text.p: ** BIRTHDAYS **
Belgian musical instrument maker and inventor of the saxophone ADOLPHE SAX was born in 1814.
The inventor of basketball JAMES A. NAISMITH was born in 1861. He was the American international physical education director at the international YMCA.
Pioneer Australian pharmacist WASHINGTON HANDLEY SOUL was born in 1865. His shops still trade.
Australian composer MAY BRAHE was born in 1884. She wrote "Bless This House" as well as many songs for recording artists PETER DAWSON and DAME NELLIE MELBA.

United States orchestra leader RAY CONNIFF was born in 1916. He had million sellers with nine albums between 1957 and 1973. His orchestra accompanied JOHNNY RAY, FRANKIE LAINE, MARTY ROBBINS and JOHNNY MATHIS. His biggest hit single was
"Somewhere, My Love" in 1966.
German-born American director MIKE NICHOLS, who won an oscar for "The Graduate", was born in 1931.
US country singer, guitarist and songwriter STONEWALL JACKSON was born in 1932. He was named after the Confederate general and his biggest cross-over hit was "Waterloo" in 1959.

American guitarist, pianist, singer and songwriter GLENN FREY was born in 1948. He played with BOB SEGER and he became a founding member of the 'Eagles' in 1971. His solo records from 1982 onwards included "The Heat Is On" (1984), "You Belong To The City" (1985) and "True Love" (1988).
** EVENTS **
1429 : HENRY VI was crowned King of England, seven years
after acceding to the throne at the age of eight months.
1813 : Mexico was proclaimed independent from Spain.
1860 : ABRAHAM LINCOLN elected president of the United
States.
1917 : After five months the third battle of Ypres
finally ended when the Canadians and Australians took Passchendaele. The advance was only five miles at a cost of at least 240,000 men.
1923 : German inflation skyrocketted. The German mark was
4.2 trillion to the US dollar. Workers could be seen taking their wages home in wheelbarrows and crates, almost as worthless as monopoly money. A loaf of bread cost 200 million marks.
1932 : In German elections, the Nazis lost 34 seats and
two million votes but still remained the largest party in the Reichstag with 196 seats.
1942 : The Church of England in the United Kingdom ended
its rule requiring women to wear hats in church.
1947 : The Prime Minister announced that Australia was to
have a permanent settlement in Antarctica.
1968 : RICHARD NIXON was elected president of the United
States, eight years after he narrowly failed to beat JOHN F. KENNEDY.
1975 : The 'Sex Pistols' had the plug pulled on their
very first concert. They were playing at London's St Martin's College of Art. There were reportedly scenes of mayhem and after ten minutes the college's social secretary called off the performance.
1984 : A Dublin High Court froze the funds of the British
mineworkers' union. The move came in the 35th week of the miners' strike, which had been declared illegal. The High court had ruled the union pay 109,000 dollars in fines within 14
days or have its assets seized.
1987 : Rail passengers at India's Patna station got more

than their train timetables on the platform television screens. The timetables flashed off and startled train travellers saw a pornographic movie on the screens instead. It's not known how long it took the commuters to notify authorities of the error.
The official explanation was simply that there had been a "mistake".
1987 : The first transcontinental solar-powered car race
from Darwin to Adelaide was won by General Motors "Sunraycer" in five days.
1991 : President of the Russian Federation BORIS YELTSIN
issued a decree banning the Communist Party in the Soviet Union and Russia. The party's property was nationalised.
1994 : Bushfires again flared across much of New South
Wales and Queensland, as wild storms swept Australia's south.
1995 : Israel buried YITZHAK RABIN, assassinated by a
fellow Jew who opposed peace with Palestinians.
